stem: A child initially thought to have gastroenteritis is found to have diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA); what is the best response to a suggestion to use the usual gastroenteritis deficit shortcut without modification?

options.text: That is appropriate because DKA usually has a smaller water deficit than the clinical assessment suggests
Use no rehydration fluids in DKA until ketones clear
Seek senior advice because children with DKA may have a greater total body water deficit than the initial clinical assessment suggests
Replace only ongoing losses because maintenance and deficit do not apply in DKA
Delay all fluids until urine ketones are measured

explanation: Seek senior advice for DKA fluid management because the total body water deficit may be greater than the initial clinical assessment suggests.

optionExplanations.A: Incorrect because DKA may involve a greater, not smaller, water deficit than first appears.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect because DKA requires careful fluid management, not withholding all rehydration until ketones clear.
optionExplanations.C: Correct because children with DKA may have a greater total body water deficit than the initial clinical assessment suggests, so senior advice is appropriate.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect because both deficit and maintenance fluid requirements still need to be considered in DKA management.
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect because fluid assessment and management should not be delayed until urine ketones are measured.
